title: Best Project Management Certifications for Beginners (2026)
dek: Five programmes, five different kinds of product — and five prices that measure five different things. What you are actually buying, and how to choose by what you want it for.

intent.primaryKeyword: best project management certifications for beginners

seo.metaDescription: The five beginner options are not the same kind of product, and their prices do not compare. What you are actually buying, and how to choose by goal.

sources.label: PMI — Certified Associate in Project Management (CAPM)
Google Project Management Professional Certificate — Coursera
Scrum.org — Professional Scrum Master I (PSM I)

body.richText: A beginner asking which project management certification to start with is usually handed the same five: the CAPM, the Google Project Management Certificate, the PSM I, the CSM, and PRINCE2 Foundation. The list is not wrong. It is arranged badly. Those five are not the same kind of product, and the prices attached to them are not the same kind of number — one is a monthly subscription to course material, one is a fee to attempt an assessment you can fail, one is a charge for renewing a credential you do not yet hold. Lined up in a column headed "cost", they invite a comparison that cannot honestly be made. So this page does something different: it sets out what each of these actually is, what your money is buying in each case, and how to choose once you can see the difference.

body.text: What these five things actually are

body.richText: The distinction that matters most is between buying teaching and buying a credential. The Google Project Management Certificate is sold as a subscription to course material: you work through it and finish with a record that you completed it. The other four are issued by organisations whose business is certifying people. That difference is not a matter of prestige, and it is not something either side has an incentive to explain to you — but it is observable. Three of the four impose a renewal obligation to keep what you have earned, which is the clearest sign that they treat it as a standing credential rather than a course you finished.

body.caption: What each programme is, and what we were able to confirm at the issuing organisation in September 2026. The classification in the middle column is CertNorth's.
headers: What kind of product it is
rows: Google Project Management Certificate
A paid course you work through — teaching, with a completion record at the end
Delivered by subscription; no prior knowledge required
CAPM (PMI)
A certification with an education requirement, maintained on a cycle
23 hours of project management education are required, and PMI's own training satisfies them
PSM I (Scrum.org)
A certification earned by passing an assessment
80 questions, 60 minutes, 85% to pass; the test password does not expire until it is used
CSM (Scrum Alliance)
A certification with a fixed renewal cycle
Renewal every two years: 20 SEUs and a US$100 fee
PRINCE2 Project Management Foundation (Version 7)
A PeopleCert qualification
A three-year renewal cycle and a requirement of 60 CPD points

richText: Note what the middle column does not do: it does not rank these. A course is not a lesser thing than a credential — it is a different purchase, and which one serves you depends on whether you are trying to learn the work or to hold something a body will vouch for. The

body.text: What your money is actually buying

richText: The recurring side is the part beginners underestimate, and the cycles in the table above are only half of it. The CAPM's is the one worth spelling out: three years, 15 PDUs, and a composition that is fixed rather than free — at least 9 must be Education and at most 6 may be Giving Back, which together account for all 15, with a minimum of 2 in each area of PMI's Talent Triangle. There is no discretionary remainder to fill with whatever is convenient. For the Google certificate and the PSM I we could not confirm whether any renewal obligation exists at all; it is widely said that neither expires, and we are not going to repeat that as fact when we have not checked it.

body.text: The one you have heard of is not on this list

richText: The PMP is absent from both tables deliberately. It is PMI's senior credential and it requires documented project experience, which is precisely what a beginner does not yet have — so putting it in a beginners' comparison makes the comparison worse, not more complete. It belongs in this article only as a destination. What PMI requires is set out in our

body.text: Which of these employers respect — and why we will not tell you

richText: This is the question every beginner actually wants answered, and it is the one we have no basis to answer. Every source that speaks to how employers treat entry-level certifications is either the organisation issuing the credential or somebody selling training for it. We have no independent measure of hiring behaviour, and we are not going to manufacture one out of impressions. What we can say is narrower and more useful: whether the profession requires certification at all is a prior question, and we take it up in

link.text: do you need a certification to be a project manager

richText: . Beyond that, the only market that matters to your decision is your own, and you can read it yourself in an evening.

items: Search the entry-level titles you would actually apply for — project coordinator, junior project manager, associate project manager — in your own city or sector
For each posting, note where certification appears: under requirements, under preferred, or only in a closing list of nice-to-haves. Those are three different asks
Note which credential is named, if any. "A project management certification" and a specific credential by name are not the same requirement
Check whether the postings naming one are the jobs you would take, or the ones you would not

body.richText: That is a reading of your market, not a statistic, and it should not be treated as one. But it answers the question for the only case you need answered, which no survey can do for you.

richText: The criterion running through all of this is not which credential is best. It is what you are trying to buy. If you want to learn the work — you have no background, and you want structure before you commit further — you are buying teaching, and the Google certificate is the one of these five sold as teaching. On the criterion that matters for a standing start, that it assumes no prior knowledge and moves at your pace, it is the gentlest way in; on a different criterion, such as holding something a certifying body maintains and stands behind, it is not the answer at all. Our fuller assessment is in

link.text: our review of the Google certificate

richText: If you want a credential rather than a course, the thing to plan for is the obligation, not the purchase: renewal is a commitment of time as much as money. If your target work is Scrum-based, the field narrows immediately to the PSM I and the CSM, and the choice between them turns on your role and on who is paying — set out in
and in our wider look at

goes further than this page does. And whether PRINCE2 is used where you work is not something we can tell you — it is exactly what the check in the previous section is for, and our

If none of that resolves it, the likelier possibility is that the question is early rather than difficult. A certification bought before you know which work you want is the one purchase here that is hard to put to use, and

link.text: how to become a project manager

richText: sets out what you can build in the meantime that no credential replaces.

body.text: Three numbers to check before you pay

body.richText: We would rather send you to the source than pretend to hold every current price. Three things are worth confirming yourself, in this order.

items: What is actually being charged. We could not confirm a current CAPM exam fee, or what it costs to obtain a CSM. Read PMI's and Scrum Alliance's own pages and see what they charge today — a price quoted anywhere else is a price from some other date

What unit the charge is in. US$49 buys a month of subscription; US$200 buys one attempt at an assessment needing 85% to pass; US$100 renews a CSM rather than buying one. Not one of those is "the price of the certification", and a figure quoted without its unit cannot be compared with anything

Whether the price applies to you. The Google figures we could confirm are for the US and Canada, and Coursera notes that prices may differ elsewhere. The PRINCE2 figure is the single package shown on the page we checked, not a universal price. Read the page for your own country before you pay

body.richText: None of this is an argument against buying one of these. It is the difference between buying something you understand and buying a number you saw in a table.
